messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 77, Vannak had spent most of his adult life in the United States, building a career as a firefighter and a reputation for steadiness under pressure. He was married, still working in a reduced capacity, and known at the station as someone who did not rattle easily. What he rarely spoke about was that, as a boy in Southeast Asia, he had lived in a civilian area that became a war zone. He could still picture one attack with unbearable precision: the flat crack of an explosion, the rush of dust, adults shouting names to find the missing, the helplessness of being small in the middle of violence that treated human beings like debris. What stayed with him was not only the danger but the feeling that people could be reduced in an instant to something handled, moved, counted. Even now, when the memory came, it was sharply detailed and strangely estranged, as if he were watching something that had happened to another child and yet feeling it in his own body at the same time.

For years he managed by not dwelling on it. More recently, the old material had been forcing its way in. At work, the sound of ambulances backing in or racing out of the station could catch him off guard; a sudden bang at a call scene, a dropped metal tool, even hearing a name that matched one shouted during the attack could pull up the past with no warning. In those moments the memory did not unfold like ordinary remembering. It arrived clear, intrusive, and unwanted, with details he had never chosen to keep so vivid. The force of this involuntary remembering seemed to confirm something he had come to fear about himself: that if he let his mind turn toward that time, he would not be able to handle what came up.

Those same moments also stirred a harsher set of judgments. When a familiar name or the shriek of an ambulance brought the attack close, he would not only remember; he would feel again the humiliating passivity of it, the old conviction that he had been reduced to an object in other people’s violence. Because he had come to believe that catastrophe could strip a person of agency without warning, ordinary sounds and fragments of speech no longer stayed ordinary for long; they caught and held his attention as possible signs that the same kind of danger was near. The more he saw himself as someone who could be overwhelmed again, the more readily the station, the street, and even casual conversation filled with reminders. He found himself thinking that somebody else would not have gotten trapped in that situation, as if even his childhood survival could be reread as personal failure. Because the sounds and names seemed to expose him so quickly to that collapse in how he saw himself, he had started treating the world as if threat were always nearby. He scanned rooms, doorways, streets, and staging areas automatically, certain that if he missed a cue he would again be caught unaware.

That vigilance had become one of several habits that now organized his days. Around the station, if an ambulance siren rose or if dispatch traffic created the feel of an emergency building, Vannak’s eyes went immediately to exits, windows, other people’s movements. At home he delayed going to bed, resisting the dark and the quiet because lying down made it easier for the images to break through. After a memory surged up, he would double down on these efforts to keep control, staying up even later or keeping himself busy so there was less room for it to return. The intrusions had taught him to treat quiet, stillness, and unguarded moments as dangerous, which is why he leaned so heavily on vigilance and not thinking. He told himself that not thinking was the only way to stay in control; if he gave the past any space, it would overwhelm him. In the same private mental space, he sometimes drifted into fantasies of revenge against the people responsible, not because he had any plan, but because imagining a reversal of power briefly interrupted the intolerable sense of having once been helpless and less than human.

These strategies brought only short relief and often tightened the problem. Nights stretched later because he avoided sleep, and the exhaustion seemed to lower his guard; when he finally lay down, the memories came even more forcefully, vivid and uninvited. His constant checking of his surroundings kept him keyed to every bang, every siren, every shouted name, so that triggers were easier to detect and harder to dismiss. The more he monitored, the more the world felt loaded with reminders. And when the memory broke through despite all his efforts, he took that as proof that he truly could not handle it, that something about him was weaker than it should be.

Over the past year this has become harder to contain. On calls involving ambulances, he has found himself briefly pulled out of the present by the old scene; afterward he is ashamed that his mind went there at all. He has become quieter with his wife at night, staying up in another room rather than explaining why he dreads the dark. What finally brought him to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but the recognition that the pattern was spreading through the small fabric of his life: work, sleep, his marriage, his sense of himself. He is frightened that if he stops holding everything so tightly, the memories will take over completely. At the same time, he is coming in because some part of him hopes that the war can become something he remembers, rather than something that keeps arriving and telling him who he is.
